Individuals from a simulated metacommunity

Source: R/individuals.R
sample_individuals.Rd

Draws individuals from the populations of a simulated metacommunity and gives each one a trait value, so that intraspecific variation and local adaptation can be studied with the T-statistics of Violle et al. (2012) (tstats()).

Usage

sample_individuals(
  x,
  n = 10,
  fraction = NULL,
  local_adaptation = 0,
  population_sd = 0,
  intraspecific_sd = 1,
  displacement = 0,
  displacement_width = NULL,
  step = NULL,
  env = NULL,
  cover = NULL,
  min_n = 1,
  founder_sd = 0,
  monopolization = 0,
  gene_flow = 1,
  source = c("traits", "evolution"),
  session_sd = 0
)

Arguments

x

An mc_sim object from simulate_metacommunity() (or an mc_evolving one from simulate_evolving_metacommunity()).

n

Number of individuals measured in each population, or all of them when the population is smaller. Ignored when fraction is given.

fraction

Optional probability that each individual is measured, so that the number measured in a population is Binomial(abundance, fraction), proportional to abundance on average.

local_adaptation

Fraction (0 to 1) of the gap between the optimum of the species and the environment of the site that each population closes; one value or one per species (named by species, or in their order). The same holds for the two standard deviations.

population_sd

Standard deviation of the deviations of populations from the species mean that do not track the environment; one value or one per species.

intraspecific_sd

Standard deviation of trait values among the individuals of a population; one value or one per species.

displacement

Strength of character displacement among the populations of a site (c in Details), relative to the selection that keeps each population near its mean without competitors; 0 (the default) for none.

displacement_width

Width w of the Gaussian competition kernel of character displacement, in units of the trait. The default is the mean niche breadth (sigma) of the species.

step

Recorded step to sample, as in record_steps; NULL (the default) uses the abundances at the last step. Several steps simulate collections on several dates: each date is sampled on its own (new individuals, drawn from the populations then), and the result gets a column step. The deviations of each population from population_sd (and founder_sd) are kept across dates, so populations change between dates only through the simulation. For evolving metacommunities, the records keep only the lineages extant at the end, so an earlier date misses species that died out later.

env

Optional environment of each site at the sampled step, or, with several steps, a matrix with one column per step (a vector is used for every date). The default is the environment of the landscape for every date; give it for simulations with env_time. With source = "evolution" the environment comes from the simulation.

cover

Optional share (0 to 1) of the abundance of each site covered by the species measured: species are taken from the most abundant down until they reach cover, and the rest are not measured, as in field protocols that measure the species making up 80% of the abundance (Pakeman & Quested 2007). NULL (the default) measures every species.

min_n

Populations with fewer individuals measured than min_n are left out, as when populations with a single individual are removed before computing T-statistics.

founder_sd

Standard deviation of the founder deviation of a population founded by a single individual (\(s_f\) in the section Founder effects and monopolization); the deviation of a population founded by \(n\) individuals has standard deviation founder_sd / sqrt(n). One value or one per species; 0 (the default) for none.

monopolization

Rate per time step (\(\rho\)) at which a population closes the gap between the optimum of its species and the environment of its site after it arrives, so that early colonists end up better adapted than late ones. One value or one per species; 0 (the default) for none.

gene_flow

Rate (\(\gamma\)) at which immigration erodes founder deviations and adaptation since arrival, per unit of migrant load: 1 (the default) when every newcomer mixes fully with the residents, 0 for no erosion. One value or one per species. Has no effect without founder_sd or monopolization.

source

Where population means come from: "traits" (the default) builds them from the optimum of each species with the arguments above; "evolution" takes them from a simulation run with evolution (evolution_control()), as the genetic mean plus the plastic part of each population at the sampled step, and draws individuals around them with the genetic plus environmental variance of each species (genetic_var + env_var, plus, for a species of several lineages, the variance among them in the site), so that the T-statistics of tstats() reflect the variation that evolved. intraspecific_sd, when given, then adds variation such as measurement error, and local_adaptation, population_sd, displacement, founder_sd, monopolization and env must keep their defaults (env is the environment at the sampled step). At a step before the last, the simulation needs record_steps with that step, which keep the genetic means (and, for evolving metacommunities, of the lineages extant at the end). Evolving metacommunities from simulate_evolving_metacommunity() are accepted too. With several evolving traits (one per niche axis), individuals are drawn from a multivariate normal with covariance \(G + E\) of their species, and intraspecific_sd takes one value or one per trait; the output then has, for each trait, the columns env_<trait> and mean_<trait> and the trait itself (named after its axis) instead of env, optimum, population_mean and trait, with the trait names in the attribute "traits". session_sd shifts each trait on its own.

session_sd

Standard deviation of an error shared by all individuals measured on the same date (step), such as a difference between measurers or calibrations; it is added to trait, not to population_mean. 0 (the default) for none.

Value

Data frame with one row per individual and the columns step (with several steps), site, species, individual (its number within the population), abundance (of the population), env (of the site), optimum (of the species), population_mean (the expected value of the population, \(m_{ij}\) above, after character displacement) and trait, and with founder_sd or monopolization also arrival (the step at which the population was founded), before trait. Populations with no individual measured are absent.

Details

The trait is the environmental optimum of species_traits(), the one that sets growth in simulate_metacommunity(). The value of individual \(k\) of species \(j\) at site \(i\) is

$$z_{ijk} = \theta_j + h_j (E_i - \theta_j) + d_{ij} + e_{ijk},$$

where \(\theta_j\) is the optimum of the species, \(E_i\) the environment of the site, \(h_j\) (local_adaptation) the fraction of the gap between them that the population closes, \(d_{ij} \sim N(0, s_p^2)\) (with \(s_p\) = population_sd) a deviation of the population that does not track the environment (drift, founder effects), and \(e_{ijk} \sim N(0, s_e^2)\) (with \(s_e\) = intraspecific_sd) the variation among individuals of a population. With local_adaptation = 0 and population_sd = 0 all populations of a species share its mean; with local_adaptation = 1 every population sits on the environment of its site and species no longer differ within a site.

With displacement > 0, the populations of each site also diverge from one another, as in ecological character displacement. Their means are the equilibrium of

$$\mu_{ij} = m_{ij} + c \sum_k p_{ik} (\mu_{ij} - \mu_{ik}) \exp\left(-\frac{(\mu_{ij} - \mu_{ik})^2}{2 w^2}\right),$$

where \(m_{ij} = \theta_j + h_j (E_i - \theta_j) + d_{ij}\) is the mean above, \(c\) is displacement, \(p_{ik}\) the share of species \(k\) among the individuals of the site and \(w\) (displacement_width) the width of a Gaussian competition kernel. Each population is pushed away from the populations close to it in trait, more so from abundant ones, and held near \(m_{ij}\), so \(c\) sets the strength of competition relative to the selection that keeps the population near \(m_{ij}\). The push from one competitor is largest at a distance \(w\) and at most \(c w e^{-1/2}\), about \(0.6 c w\). The equilibrium is found by damped fixed-point iteration from \(m_{ij}\), with steps of \(1 / (1 + c)\). Populations with the same \(m_{ij}\), as with local_adaptation = 1 and no population_sd, are not pushed apart, since the push is symmetric. With \(c > 1\), however, the equilibrium with equal means is unstable: populations whose \(m_{ij}\) differ even slightly end up about \(w \sqrt{2 \log c}\) apart, and several equilibria can exist, of which the iteration finds the one reached from \(m_{ij}\). The size of the displacement therefore grows with \(c\) only slowly once \(c\) exceeds 1.

The traits of individuals are drawn after the simulation and do not feed back on the dynamics: abundances are those of the species means. The function describes the pattern that local adaptation would leave in samples of individuals, not its demographic consequences.

Founder effects and monopolization

population_sd and local_adaptation treat every population of a species alike, whatever its history. Two further mechanisms make the mean of a population depend on when and how it was founded, from the colonisation history recorded by simulate_metacommunity() (see colonisation_history()). Both need the last step (step = NULL). For a population founded at step \(a_{ij}\) by \(n_{ij}\) individuals, with migrant load \(L_{ij}\) since then and \(T\) steps in the simulation:

  • Founder effects (founder_sd, \(s_f\)): the population starts from the mean of its founders, a deviation \(f_{ij} \sim N(0, s_f^2 / n_{ij})\) from the species mean, so few founders deviate more. founder_sd is thus the deviation of a population founded by a single individual. The deviation persists, and gene flow erodes it toward the species mean: it is multiplied by \(g_{ij} = \exp(-\gamma L_{ij})\), where \(\gamma\) is gene_flow.

  • Monopolization (monopolization, a rate \(\rho\) per step): after arrival the population adapts to its site, closing a share \(u_{ij}\) of the gap between the optimum of the species and the environment. Without gene flow, \(u_{ij} = 1 - \exp(-\rho t_{ij})\), where \(t_{ij} = T - a_{ij}\) is the age of the population. Newcomers pull it back toward the species mean, so \(du/dt = \rho (1 - u) - \gamma \bar m u\), with \(\bar m = L_{ij} / t_{ij}\) the mean migrant load per step since arrival, whose solution is \(u_{ij} = \rho / (\rho + \gamma \bar m) [1 - \exp(-\rho t_{ij} - \gamma L_{ij})]\): adaptation tends to a balance between selection and migration instead of reaching the environment. Early colonists have had longer to adapt and end up closer to the environment of their site than late arrivals, which is the evolution-mediated priority effect of the monopolization hypothesis (Urban & De Meester 2009; De Meester et al. 2016). The gap between early and late colonists is largest when \(1 / \rho\) is close to the spread of arrival times; much faster adaptation brings every population to the balance and erases it. It combines with local_adaptation (\(h_j\)) so that the share of the gap closed is \(h_j + (1 - h_j) u_{ij}\).

The mean of the population is then \(\theta_j + [h_j + (1 - h_j) u_{ij}] (E_i - \theta_j) + d_{ij} + g_{ij} f_{ij}\), before character displacement. Use population_sd for deviations unrelated to history (drift at equilibrium, unmeasured microhabitat), local_adaptation for adaptation that every population reaches whatever its age, founder_sd for random deviations set at colonisation and kept by isolation, and monopolization for adaptation that depends on arrival order. The two arrival-dependent mechanisms leave different signatures: founder deviations are random in direction and largest in populations founded by few individuals and receiving few immigrants, while monopolization moves populations toward the environment of their site, more so the earlier they arrived. With gene_flow = 0 neither is eroded. Erosion of founder deviations multiplies them by the product of the shares of residents over the steps, approximated by \(\exp(-L)\); monopolization assumes newcomers arrived at a constant rate since arrival, \(\bar m\), rather than following the steps in which they actually came.

Limits of the two mechanisms:

  • They need the last step (step = NULL): the colonisation history is recorded at the end of the simulation only, so a recorded step other than the last gives an error.

  • They need arrivals spread over time. Without extirpation and with little dispersal, every population is founded at the start or during seed_steps, all have about the same age, and monopolization cannot separate early from late colonists. Use extirpation > 0 and some dispersal, so that populations are lost and founded again throughout the simulation, and check the spread of arrival times with colonisation_history().

  • The gap between early and late colonists does not grow without bound with monopolization: it is largest when \(1 / \rho\) is close to the spread of arrival times, and much faster adaptation brings every population to the balance with migration and erases it. In a simulation of 200 steps, the difference in the share of the gap closed between colonists that arrived before and after the median rose from 0.14 at \(\rho = 0.002\) to 0.40 at 0.02 and fell to 0.11 at 0.2. Choose the range of monopolization (for instance, a prior in approximate Bayesian computation) from the arrival times of the simulation.

  • Like the other trait deviations, they do not feed back on the dynamics: early colonists are better matched to their site but do not grow faster or compete better, so the demographic part of the monopolization hypothesis is not simulated.

References

Violle, C., Enquist, B. J., McGill, B. J., Jiang, L., Albert, C. H., Hulshof, C., Jung, V., & Messier, J. (2012). The return of the variance: intraspecific variability in community ecology. Trends in Ecology & Evolution, 27, 244–252. doi:10.1016/j.tree.2011.11.014

Pakeman, R. J., & Quested, H. M. (2007). Sampling plant functional traits: what proportion of the species need to be measured? Applied Vegetation Science, 10, 91–96. doi:10.1111/j.1654-109x.2007.tb00507.x

Urban, M. C., & De Meester, L. (2009). Community monopolization: local adaptation enhances priority effects in an evolving metacommunity. Proceedings of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences, 276, 4129–4138. doi:10.1098/rspb.2009.1382

De Meester, L., Vanoverbeke, J., Kilsdonk, L. J., & Urban, M. C. (2016). Evolving perspectives on monopolization and priority effects. Trends in Ecology & Evolution, 31, 136–146. doi:10.1016/j.tree.2015.12.009

colonisation_history() for the arrival history; tstats() for the T-statistics; subsample_individuals() and trait_rarefaction() for the same sampling schemes on real data.

Examples

set.seed(1)
tree <- treeshapesim::sim_tree_shape(15)
sim <- simulate_metacommunity(landscape_implicit(10), species_traits(tree),
                              competition_matrix(tree, "none"), n_steps = 100,
                              seed_steps = 1:5)
ind <- sample_individuals(sim, n = 10, local_adaptation = 0.5, intraspecific_sd = 2)
head(ind)
#>    site species individual abundance      env  optimum population_mean    trait
#> 1 site1      t2          1        79 47.76196 46.10733        46.93465 50.64409
#> 2 site1      t2          2        79 47.76196 46.10733        46.93465 44.09239
#> 3 site1      t2          3        79 47.76196 46.10733        46.93465 48.50888
#> 4 site1      t2          4        79 47.76196 46.10733        46.93465 47.59176
#> 5 site1      t2          5        79 47.76196 46.10733        46.93465 43.93408
#> 6 site1      t2          6        79 47.76196 46.10733        46.93465 44.05996
# arrival-dependent deviations need colonisation after the start: extirpation and dispersal
sim2 <- simulate_metacommunity(landscape_implicit(20), species_traits(tree),
                               competition_matrix(tree, "phylo"), n_steps = 200,
                               dispersal = 0.005, extirpation = 0.01)
# founder effects: deviations set at colonisation, larger with few founders, eroded by
# immigration
founders <- sample_individuals(sim2, founder_sd = 2, intraspecific_sd = 0.5)
# monopolization: early colonists close more of the gap to the environment of their site
mono <- sample_individuals(sim2, monopolization = 0.02, intraspecific_sd = 0)
closed <- (mono$population_mean - mono$optimum) / (mono$env - mono$optimum)
early <- mono$arrival <= stats::median(mono$arrival)
c(early = mean(closed[early]), late = mean(closed[!early]))
#>     early      late 
#> 0.7385448 0.3317174
